speechtext: Upon the orders of the day:

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to read an item in the ' Citizen ' of to-day, and found a question upon it which I will ask the hon. the Minister of Finance, (Mr. Fielding) to answer. It reads, as follow's:

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Fielding Returns-Tariff Conference at Albany ends in most Friendly Manner-Reported that probability of Tariff War has receded and a Settlement regarded as likely-Conference occupied Whole of Yesterday but no Conclusion was reached, says President Taft. Canadian Minister has left for Ottawa and may go to Washington the end of month.
(Special to the ' Citizen/)
Albany, N.Y., March 20.-There will probably be no tariff war between the United Mr. ARTHURS
States and Canada. The prospect for commercial peace with the Dominion is more favourable to-night than it has been at any time since the president caused it to he understood that the situation was critical.
By joint agreement between President Taft and Hon. W. S. Fielding, the Canadian Minister of Finance, the following statement was given out from the state executive mansion this evening for publication:-
' The President and Mr. Fielding were in conference in respect to the tariff to-dav for several hours. No conclusion was reached, hut the situation remains that of friendly negotiations/
Despite the late hour at which the University Club dinner ended Mr. Fielding and Mr. Charles M. Pepper, who is here from Washington as the representative of the state department, were at the executive mansion at half past nine o'clock this morning. They immediately went into private ' conference with Mr. Taft and remained closeted with him until he had to leave them to keep his engagement to attend church with Governor Hughes. The Canadian minister and Mr. Pepper returned together to the Ten Eyck hotel, chatting in a manner that indicated amicable relations, but they returned to the governor's official residence in time to resume the conference with the president after luncheon, to which Earl Grey and Mr. Fielding as well as the president had been invited as the guests of Governor and Mrs. Hughes.
After luncheon the conference was resumed, and it continued until four o'clock in the afternoon, when the president, by reason of an appointment of long standing, kept an afternoon tea engagement at the house of his friends, Mr. and Mrs. Ward. Mr. Fielding and Mr. Pepper again returned to the hotel. They repaired to the apartments occupied by the Dominion Minister of Finance and busied themselves in going over certain of the tariff schedules with a view of reaching some basis agreeable to both sides whereby the president would he justified in withholding the operation against Canadian imports of the maximum tariff as prescribed by the Payne-Aldrich law after March 31.
I wish to ask the Minister of Finance whether that statement is substantially correct and whether there was a conference between the President of the United States and our Finance Minister in Albany yesterday (Sunday) re tariff matters, as alleged in the despatch read? Was the invitation of the president, which was accepted by the government, for a Sunday conference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: At the invitation of the President of the United States, I visited Albany and had the honour and the pleasure of meeting that gentleman on both Saturday and Sunday. We discussed matters which I trust will work for the peace, order and good government of these two nations; there could be no better Sunday work.

In the New York 'World' of Friday, March 18, I see a dispatch speaking of the proposed treaty between Japan and the United States, part of which is:
England wishes to get away from her treaty with Japan, and Japan, it is said here to-day, is ready bo let her go at the expiration of the Lansdowne-Hayashi agreement. Japan is desirous, however, of having a government support her in the Orient without committing her against any nation.
The reason for this is that Japan does not feel capable of taking care of the commercial and industrial feature of China, but she also has her doubts as to the motives behind offers of certain European governments. With the United States ready to develop the far east in accordance with every provision of American ' commercial equality ' and without ulterior motives of aggrandisement, Japan feels that China's future and freedom from contention are assured.	[DOT]

The points to be added on the new proposal, not included in the Root-Takahiia agreement, and which could not be embraced by the latter, even in its vague wording, are these:
1.	Consolidation in Asia, especially along the Pacific shores.
2.	To include Great Britain if she desires to become a party, through her alliance with the empire, by a triangulation of interests, or dissociate England entirely without in any way jeopardizing British interests.
3.	Further definition of fisheries rights.
4.	That the jeopardy of the rights of either nation requiring safeguarding of common and mutual interests and rights is not to be construed as open belligerents but a bid. for either arbitration or other outlet.
5.	That the powers signatory to the Hay note do not figure in any way in the motives behind this new pact other than to share all the [DOT]benefits to be derived by a direct understanding between two nations politically, diplomatically and commercially identified wTith the Pacific basin, namely, Japan and the United States.
6.	Japan will agree to maintain peace so long as her own sovereignty is not menaced.
7.	Japan, in the event that the United States will concede the moral right to guide and control Chinese Manchuria and the Pacific basin in general, does not oppose Russia, nor does she seek any right other than that of mutual friend to all those interested; m the event of difficulties, the matter will then be referred to the participating governments for settlement.
In courtesy to the powers they will be acquainted with the fact that Japan wishes to come to a more settled and definite amicable understanding with the United States.
Might I ask the government, in view of the fact that in this despatch the Pacific ocean is regarded as practically a sea concerning which the United States, Japan and Great Britain (Great Britain, I presume, being more especially interested through Canada, Australia and New Zealand) shall have control, if the government have the intention of taking any steps towards safeguarding the rights of Canada, through the empire, in this proposed treaty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have to inform my hon. friend that we have received no invitation at all from the imperial authorities upon this subject.

speechtext: Is the Finance Minister in a position to give any information as to what progress, if any, he afM the government have made in their negotiations with President Taft over tariff matters?

House in committee on Bill (No. 128) to incorporate the James Bay and Eastern Railway Company-Mr. Girard.
On section 11,

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND EASTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: We had a good deal of discussion over this clause in the committee. I understand that the hon. minister was present when the Bill went through. From recollection the clause provided that the company might acquire electric power and energy and sell surplus power 'but had not the right to build dams or generate electric powpr. I am at a loss to understand why they should require the right to dispose of surplus power if they are only to get such as they need for theij own purposes.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND EASTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
This condition might arise. They might need 10,000 horse-power for the purposes of their undertaking. They might have to buy from some one who had 11,000 horse-power to sell and they would have to buy the whole 11,000. This Bill would give them the right to sell the surplus 1,000.
Mr. LANCASTER, The words 'not by expropriation' are to go in.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND EASTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND EASTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: That is rather a weak argument. If the railway required a quantity of power and got- one horse-power more than it required, it would not be a great hardship on the company if it were not able to dispose of that. It looks very much as if something was lurking behind this apparently innocent language. It looks like an attempt to get control of water-powers which will not be used necessarily for the operation of the railway as it should be.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND EASTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Does the clause read now 'in the municipalities through which the railway is authorized to be built' or 'in the municipalities through which the railway is built'?	'

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: JAMES BAY AND EASTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The clause reads as follow's:
11. For the purposes of its undertaking and subject to the provisions of section 247 of the Railway Act the company may acquire but not by expropriation, electric or other power, or energy, which may be transmitted and delivered to any place in the municipalities through which the railway is authorized to be built, and may receive, transform, transmit, distri-Mr. OLIVER.
bute and supply such power or energy in any form, and may dispose of the surplus thereof, and may collect rates and charges therefor; but no such rate or charge shall be demanded or taken until it has been approved of by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, who may also revise such rates and charges from time to time.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND EASTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: In other Bills of a similar character we have confined them to the municipalities through which the road is built and not through which it is authorized to ibe built, the reason being that the railway must first build its road before engaging in the business of distributing electric power. Otherwise the company might never build its railway and simply become a transmission and distributing power company. I would think that we should follow the practice adopted with respect to other Bills and 'strike out the words 'authorized tp build'.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND EASTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I thought that was the amendment made in committee. We had quite a discussion there. Attention was drawn to the fact that the railway might build two miles only, though authorized to build a line a thousand miles long. Under the power given by this Bill, it would have the right to distribute electricity along the whole of its authorized line through all the municipalities. There was evidently some mistake, for the Bill has not been reported as the committee intended.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND EASTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: According to that amendment, this company would have the right to enter into any municipality and distribute electricity in competition with a municipal plant and perhaps destroy it, or the municipality might have to sell out its plant to this company. I understood that it was the intention to have these Bills amended in such a way that a com- * pany such as this could not enter a municipality and interfere with a municipal plant.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND EASTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Do I understand the hon.
member for Westmorland has moved to strike out these words?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: JAMES BAY AND EASTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND EASTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND EASTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Before the Bill was passed in the committee, we had several Bills in which these words ' authorized to be built ' appeared, and in every case we

changed them. In the Rainy River Bill we had this clause again, and we changed the wording so that this Bill stands alone in that respect. It will be advisable, 1 think, for the promoter of this Bill to consent to this change. This must have got in merely by inadvert-ance. We have adopted a definite practice in that matter, and it is the duty of this committee, I submit, to insist that in some way it be made right. I am disposed to press the objection, and, if the promoter of the Bill will not consent to what has. been the uniform practice, then to ask that the committee rise and report progress, so that notice may be given.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND EASTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The hon. member (Mr. Girard), who is in charge of the Bill, is not present. Of course, if there are amendments to be made, it would be better to move that the committee rise and report progress, that the usual notice may be given. The other point of view may be worthy of consideration, and it is this: A railway line-say this railway line-is to be built. If you confine it to the power on which the line is built, you might make the rule so rigid that they could not use it to run the road. House in committee on Bill (No. 108) to incorporate the Rainy River Radial Railway Company.-Mr. Conmee.
On section 9-power to operate telegraph and telephone lines.
Is that amended, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It does not appear so in the copy before me.

I think that after the word * may ' were to be inserted the words ' for the purposes of its undertaking, and,' .making it read: ' The company may, for the purposes of its undertaking, and subject to the provisions of the Railway Act, construct and operate telegraph and telephone lines,' and so on. I move that these words be inserted. I do not think it is usual to give a railway company the right to do a telephone and telegraph business. I do not think my hon. friend (Mr. Conmee) desires more than that they should have power to carry on a telephone business in connection with and for the purposes of their railway.
I think that is correct.

Amendment agreed to.
On section 10-express business.

I think that the railway companies, when they have the express business entirely under their own control sometimes act in a not very generous way with the public. They often compel shippers to send goods by express and pay a much higher figure if they want them taken proper care of and sent through rapidly. There are many advantages in combining the ownership of railway and express services, but there are some disadvantages to the public which are very considerable. Take the case of a line passing through our section of the country; when it was in its original ownership, there was an express company different from the railway company. The railway company was obliged to haul the express cars, but the express company could make its own contract. The public had much better service then than they have had since the express company was bought up by the railway company. The railway and express are now controlled by the Canadian Pacific railway. The people' have to pay much higher figures for their express, and they have less advantages than they had under the old system. For instance, the company will not deliver express in the villages. The express matter is dumped at the station, and the individuals for whom it is intended may not receive notice before several days. And then they have to go down to the station for it. The charge is made much higher. For instance, where they carried express, it was 60 cents a hundred to Toronto, now it is 75 cents. These are all exactions from the nublic, and I thought it was due to the fact that when the railway company took over the express business and were carrying freight and express, they could charge whatever they pleased.
On section 12,
I would ask the Minister of Railways if this is the usual clause. I was not able to attend the committee in which the change was made.

I think this clause is somewhat new, in that it introduces the words ' not by expropriation.' We did not have that in the old clause. We have for some years gone on the understanding that the provisions of the Railway Act, as the particular clauses were drawn, did not apply to these Bills with regard to expropriation. But to make sure we put in these words ' not by expropriation.'

My understanding of that clause in the Railway Committee was this: There is in another subsection a further amendment to that clause, which stipulates that they -shall not buiid such works on the Rainy river, which is the only navigable river in the vicinity. I did not understand that the words ' not by expropriation ' were going to be inserted in that subsection 2. I think that is going a little too far. I think that subsection ought to be satisfactory, and such powers of expropriation as the Railway Act confers ought to be allowed.
Wasn't that 'agreed to in the Railway Committee?

That is the way I understood it. What good purpose is to be served by using the words, when the clause itself excludes them from the only navigable stream that could be dealt with under their charter?
There may be other water-powers that they could expropriate.

They are given authority to use a water-power and sell the surplus, but they can only do it subject to the Railway Act. What good purpose could be served? It is only depriving the public of the use of that power. It is not injuring the companies to anv great extent, but it is depriving the public of the opportunity of utilizing the power. Every one knows that a railway does not use all its power every day. In the winter season when ii has to contend with snow and ice, it has to use nearly double the force it would at other times. Now why leave that force idle? The public interest is absolutely protected. The company cannot deal with it except under the control of the board, and they 'are excluded by Act from dealing with the important stream in the district where navigation might be affected. Surely the public interest is amply protected without putting in that restriction.

The hon. gentleman asks what good purpose was to be served. In the Railway Committee we thought that there might be other water-powers than the one specifically mentioned, and that the same rule should apply to all. There must be a principle, there must not be any picking, and choosing between different powers. We thought that both these amendments were necessary. The committee thought that this company was to be subject to the Railway Act, and that they should not go into the water-power business, but only into the business of developing electricity for the railway and that they should not have the right to expropriate any water-power. Then because the Rainy river is a navigable stream, and the

Dominion government might have some control over it, to be consistent, the committee said that ' not by expropriation,' would not necessarily cover the Rainy river, because the Rainy river is navigable. And so, to carry out the principle entirely, and protect the public both as regards the Dominion authority and provincial authority, the committee almost unanimously came to the conclusion that both these amendments should be adopted as they now stand.

My own opinion is that none of these Railway Bills should be given any right to expropriate the water-powers of anybody. If I owned a water-power, if I got on the ground first, I don't think any other person ought to have a right to come in and expropriate it, and use it for the same purpose I was going to use it for. They ought to make some arrangement with me. I do not think they ought to have the right to expropriate water-powers on the right of way for the railway. If they expropriate sufficient for the right of way, I do not think it should include the water-power. It is not needed for the right of way of the railway. It is supposed to be outside of it altogether. I think that is a pretty safe ground to take.

I was very glad to hear my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) make the state-
MARCH 21, ll)b>
ment that he did. I believe the time has come when we should curtail the powers that we give under these different railway charters, and I hope that next session when these different railway companies come before this House for incorporation the Minister of Railways and Canals will lay down the principle that we will grant them railway charters but we will not grant them water-power rights in connection with the railway in any particular whatever, and that if they want water-powers let the same people, if they choose, form a water-power company and let us deal with them as a water-power company simply. There is no doubt in my mind that there has been a large number of charters put through this House with these water-power privileges attached in which we have been incorporating water-power companies and giving them privileges because they came before us as railway companies, that we would not have given if we had known clearly what their intents were. By these charters they may be enabled to secure water-powers and build only a minimum amount of the railway. The feeling generally throughout the country and on both sides of this House, I believe, is that the time has come when no more of these natural resources of the country should be given to railway corporations. I have supported some of them in the House this session simply because I did not feel that it was advisable or good policy at the end of the session to refuse one company what we have already granted to other companies during the present session, hut as far as I am concerned, at the coming session I will oppose the granting of these privileges to any of the railway companies that come to us seeking incorporation.

I do not quarrel with the general principle that has been enunciated by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), but there is a good deal of suspicion in the minds of hon. members of this House that because you say in a railway charter that the company may acquire and utilize a water-power thereby you give them the right to take or expropriate that waterpower. I deny that. You do not give them any such right, and no hon. member of this House can point to a single case in this country where a water-power has been developed or utilized by virtue of any such right given by a railway charter. You are giving companies the right to operate water-powers in connection with their system, and under the restrictions imposed in the public interest by the Railway Act instead of compelling them to carry on two sets of business, keep two sets of books and have two different organizations. That is all you do accomplish by making this
condition. I am not going to contend that the amendments should be changed because an hon. gentleman has stated that he understood them a little different from what I did. I do not think it makes any difference whatever to' this company. I do not think they are prejudiced by that clause going in, but this suspicion that you are and have been giving railway companies powers that are inimical to the public interest, and that you are creating a monopoly with regard to the acquisition and operation of water-powers is all a mistake. I do not want to use a stronger expression.
It depends on the view point.

It does not depend on the view point. It is impossible for a railway company under the powers of the Railway Act to take these water-powers. They cannot do it, and all you are doing is to compel them to maintain two separate organizations. 1 do not think that it is in the public interest that such should be done.

If the water-power is on the right of way do they not acquire it? They expropriate the right of way, and the water-power goes with it. Take such a case as that of the Lake of the Woods where the stream crosses right underneath the railway, and where the water-power is within the limits of the right of way. Surely the railway company becomes the possessor of it?

No, I have in a previous debate answered that point. There are several places where the Canadian Pacific railway, and the Canadian Northern railway cross important water-powers, but neither of these companies can develop these water-powers. At Eagle river and at Wabi-goon river the Canadian Pacific railway cross right over the head of the falls. The line of railway could not have been located better for the purpose of controlling the water-power on the Wabigoon river, as far as a railway line can control it, yet the company have no control over that waterpower. It is developed by another company altogether. The railway company never developed it, and never pretended to have any rights in the water-power. They did not secure their right of way under such conditions as to give them that right. They got their right of way from the province of Ontario, and in all the patents that are issued these water-powers are reserved. There is no case of conveying to a railway company in the deed for the right of way any right or title to the water-powers on

such right of way. It has not been done in any case that I know of, and if it were done the railway company could not develop the water-power, because you would require the right to raise the water, to build dams, intakes, and outlets, which would extend beyond the limits of any right of way. At the Lake of the' Woods the railway crosses three different branches of the Winnipeg river as it discharges from the lake, and it crosses over the head of the falls in each case. Yet these powers are developed by other people. The Lake of the Woods Milling Company controls one, the Mather Milling Company another, and Kenora another. The railway company have never pretended to have any claim on those water-powers.
Why do you want this power in the Bill?
There is no good purpose compelling any set of men to keep double books, a double staff, and a double organization. I do not see any sense in it.

All of these difficulties were advanced in the committee, and considered there. In my judgment too much care cannot be taken in the granting of these railway charters as far as the granting of water-powers is concerned. I believe that all conflict of authority between the province and the Dominion in regard to these powers has been very carefully guarded against in the wording of this Bill, and fully considered. It seems to me it ought not to be interfered with now.'
On subclause 2,

I wish to express the gratification I have at hearing the changed views of the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) with regard to the acquisition under a Railway Bill of the use of Dominion water-powers. I only hope he will continue to be a convert to that view and will not take up the time of the House bv introducing such Bills as this (which apparently have as their object not- the building of railways but the acquisition of the most valuable water-powers in Ontario. This Bill as originally introduced transgressed every doctrine that the hon. gentleman has ad vanced because it gave the promoters the absolute right to -build! dams in the Rainy fiver to obstruct navigation, to put in locks and operate them to the exclusion of public use. I am glad the -hon. gentleman has' at _last become a convert to the -doctrine that water-powers should he held for the people and used for the people.

I am pleased indeed if I have been able to satisfy my hon. friend. This Bill, however, was not introduced by me; my name was put on it and I have done my best to make it a perfect Bill. The clauses which the -chairman has just read which are guarding the public interest were moved not by the hon. gentleman but by myself.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

House again in committee on Bill (No. Ill) respecting the Dominion Millers' Association.-Mr. Harris.
On section 2, membership.
We are giving great powers, practically creating a trust, and it should be open to any one in the business under certain conditions to join the association.
Any man engaged^ in the business of milling is entitled to join.
That Would be all right if it was in the Bill, but the wording of the clause is that he is eligible.

I do not believe that the hon. gentleman if he was a member of an association would want every one to come into it unless he had some say as to who should join. As I understand every miller in the country is eligible.
I understand it is the same as in the old Bill and the difficulty then was to get them to join.

It seems that there are some 180 members, small millers, &c., and the idea that a man wishing to become a member should put in his application recommended by two other members of the association, so that no disreputable person should become a member. The executive passes on the membership the same as in any other company.
Could there not be some means by which a party introduced by two or three members would have a right to become a member?

The law clerk has pointed out that sections 6 and 7 ought to be consolidated, that there is a little repetition. He suggests, and I move, that in clause 7, subclause 2, after the word 'consist' in the first line the word 'only' should
57T3

be inserted, and in clause 6 all except the first two lines should be struck out, and then as subclause 3 we should insert:
Ordinary members shall consist of such persons only as are-
That does not change the purpose of the Bill, it simply puts the two' paragraphs into one with a sub-paragraph defining who are participating members and who are ordinary members.

I do not think there should be any objection to such a clause as the hon. member (Mr. J. Haggart) has suggested, providing that no application was refused when it was confirmed by two members of the association.

The only objection I see to that is that it seems to be contrary to the usual usage of associations and joint stock companies. In this way the company would have no voice as to who should become members.
I am not pressing the point, but we are really creating a trust.
Would it not be a greater trust if you admitted all the owners?
No, because it would be open to every person in the business. Of course, it would be a greater trust as against the public, but as against the mill owners it would not be.

By the terms of the by-law the executive committee must pass upon a man's application, they have power to reject a man. This Bill was carefully considered, and the trust aspect was greatly eliminated in clause 11. I suggested that they should not have power to purchase mills.

The clause is not framed se as to meet the wishes of the promoter. As I understand his desire is that all millers should be admitted, but the wording is only such persons as according to bylaws hereafter to be adopted are declared eligible. If the company passed a by-law declaring that no one is eligible, then you would have a close corporation.

My hon. friend does not quite seize the meaning of the section. If he will read section 7, and the warding is not changed under the amendment of the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Glarke), he will see that such persons only as are the owners or lessees of a mill, farmers and grain growlers shall be eligible. And in addition such other persons as are by bylaw hereinafter provided. But the by-law has nothing to do with the classes I have mentioned. They are eligible by the Act. * The others are to be eligible by bylaw.
Does the hon. minister interpret the Bill to mean that all per sons of the classes enumerated are eligible to become members?

They are not shut out by the statute. Their entrance might be made so difficult that it would be hard for them to get in, but by the statute they are not shut out. The hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) was quite correct in saying that the arrangement for entering the association is that two members must endorse the application. Then it is submitted to the executive committee and they pass upon it, and the impression is that they are only too glad to get everybody in they can.

This goes further than
the section in the present Act. Under the present Act only millers are entitled to become members. This extends to farmers as well. We are not limiting what they have but rather extending it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The motion of the hon. member for Essex is that clauses 6 and 7 be consolidated to read as follows:
Section 7 of the said Act is repealed and the following is substituted:-
The members of the association shall consist of two classes:	(a) Participating members, (b) Ordinary members.
2.	The participating members shall consist of such members of the association as subscribe for and are allotted one or more shares of the capital stock of the association, the issue of which is provided for by section 3 of this Act, and such shares shall be entitled to preferred cumulative dividends to an amount not exceeding ten per cent per annum.
Ordinary members shall consist of such persons only as are owners of a mill for the manufacture of flour, meal or other similar commodities, or lessees of such a mill actually carrying on the business of milling therein, farmers and grain-growers and such other persons as are by by-law hereafter provided for.

I want clearly to understand the distinction between ordinary members and the others. An ordinary member, I understand, receives no dividends and pays nothing for the stock. The others are stock-holders and receive dividends.
That is right.

When this matter was un for discussion last, it was referred back

to the committee. May I ask the Minister of Agriculture, who is taking care of the farmers in particular, if their interests have been well guarded. When it was discussed in the House on a former occasion, the suggestion was made that possibly a further combine-if it may be called a combine-of the smaller millers of Canada would be detrimental to the interests of the farming community in the purchase of offal and the products of the ordinary mill. I am not offering criticism or objection further than to ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) if, in his opinion, the farmers' interests are well taken care of, and it is clear that this will not be a combine of the millers against the farmers' interests.

I am a member of the Private Bills Committee to which this Bill was referred back. The committee referred to a special subcommittee. I was not a member of that subcommittee, but I know what discussions went on there and was present at. some of them. The question of the possibility of a combine, I think, is the most- important question in connection with this Bill. The other provisions affect the future stock-holders or the present members of the Millers' Association, and I shall not give an opinion upon these because I think they are largely the concern of these people themselves. The possibility of a combine, however, has been attempted to be guarded against by an addition to_clause 11 of the Bill providing as follows:
-if the association in any way fixes the prices at which its members shall buy or sell grain or other commodities in such a way as would have made the members of the association liable to the provisions of the Criminal Code or any other Act had they individually agreed together to the like effect, such members as acquiesce therein shall he liable under the provisions of the said Code or other Act, notwithstanding that such fixing of the price of grain or other commodities is the act of the association in the same way as if they had individually agreed together to do such acts.
I do not give a legal opinion, not being a lawyer, but this amendment seems to provide that if this association should take any action in the way of making a combine, each member of the association will be liable under the ordinary lawT.
Is not that what the law now provides, even without this clause?

I understand that the Criminal Code applies to individuals making what is considered by the law to he a combine. If the association, as an association, were to make such an arrangement, it is thought possible the criminal law might not apply-I do not say that it would Mr. BLAIN.
or that it would not. But this makes it apply. Under these circumstances, it seems to me, without presuming to give a legal opinion, that the public will be in no worse position by reason of the passing of this Act. If that be the case, the danger of a combine is provided against.

I opposed this Bill before, and cited a case, but, I am free to admit, on information given me which was not correct. I believe the railway company was involved, not the Millers' Association. I understand that the rate given in the case I referred to was exactly the same rate that the Miller's Association was paying, and that they encountered the same difficulty as I did-that the railway company would not guarantee to put the freight through in any given time, not even in six weeks or three months. I was told of an instance of grain ordered from the west to be delivered in Ontario, which was /not received for about three months. I would regard the Bill as distinctly beneficial to the agriculturists of Ontario to-day. And for this reason: The more western grain is purchased to be ground in mills in Ontario, the larger the amount of offal will be available for the Ontario farmers, and our farmers are principally feeders whose great requirement is more feed, more grain for their stock. To-day, feed can be got only in Ontario, or in the wrest, but principally in the west. Sometimes, you can get only a portion of a carload, if, instead of a few millions of bushels of grain brought down in the year, that was increased to twenty times as many, there would be twenty times the amount of feed to be had here. And the feed we get from the mills here is a better quality for feeding purposes-at least we think so-than what we get from the west.
Bill reported, and read the third time and passed.

When any private Bill is returned from the Senate with amendments the same not being merely verbal or unimportant such amendments are previous to the second reading referred to the standing committee to which such Bill was originally referred.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Royal Military College Act, chapter 43 of the Revised Statutes, 190(i, by repealing section 7 and substituting therefor the following:-
7. The salaries, pay and allowances of the commandant and of the superior and subordinate staffs of the college shall be as fixed from time to time by the Governor in Council. -Sir Frederick Borden.

Mr. Chairman, this resolution is introduced for the purpose of founding upon it a Bill to amend the Royal Military College Act. The object, as indicated, is to leave to the Governor General in Council the fixing of the salaries. To-day, as a matter of fact, the salaries paid to the professors in the Royal Military College are all fixed by order in council, excepting that of commandant. It is proposed also by this Bill to withdraw the limitations as to the total amount of money to be expended in the college. There have been several amendments from time to time increasing the amount, which was limited m the first place by the Act, and later on increased as the college has grown and the expenses have increased, and it seemed to me that instead of having to come to parliament every few years, it would be better to leave the adjustment of the amount of salaries and of the expenses to the Governor General in Council. Each year after parliament assembles, a statement is laid before parliament under the law, and it is proposed to continue this part of the Act.
Would the minister kindly read the section?

The details of such salaries shall appear in the annual report laid before parliament by the minister.
That part of the clause is continued. 1 will read the proposed Bill.
Would the minister read what the law is now?

I will read the law as it is, and then I will read the proposed amendment. The existing law is:
The salary of the commandant shall not exceed $3,200 a year, and the salaries of the staff-adjutant, professors, instructors, assistant instructors and staff shall be fixed and may be readjusted from time to time by the Governor in Council, and shall not exceed the total sum of $30,000.
It is now proposed to give the Governor in Council unlimited power as to the salary of the commandant.

Yes, just as with regard to other professors. The Auditor General has pointed out that in the last two or three sessions the amounts voted have been in excess of the amounts authorized by the Act, but of course this has been done with the consent of parliament.
Does the minister consider increasing the salaries?

No, except in the case of the commandant. In connection with the general staff, which has been arranged in conjunction with the war office as part of the military scheme, it has been found desirable that an officer of a higher grade and standing should be at the head of the college. We must have a first-class officer, who has passed the staff college in England with a first-class certificate, and must pay him what he would be paid in the army.
What is the total amount of salaries now paid?
With allowances, about $51,000.
Is it wise to give the Governor in Council unlimited power in regard to salaries? Would it not be well to place a limit, say of $60,000.

I accept the suggestion, although I thought there were sufficient safeguards through the voting of estimates by parliament each year. I am content to put the amount at $55,000 or $60,000 but I think it would be better at $60,000.
What is the pay of the staff adjutant?

I would impress on the minister that it is important to have a staff adjutant of high qualifications and great tact. He has to act as the intermediary between the commandant and the cadets, to make the orders of the commandant effective, and should be a man of very high qualifications. I know that Staff Adjutant Lafferty was such a man and did more work than he was paid for, and the minister should always have a first-class man as staff adjutant.

I quite agree with my horn, friend. Captain Kaulbach, the present staff adjutant, is a son of the late Senator Kaulbach, a graduate of the Royal Military College, and well suited to perform those difficult duties.

I see that in the school that is being founded in Australia

a condition is imposed that the cadets shall he at the absolute disposition of the country which gives them their education. Would it not be well to make it obligatory on these cadets to place themselves at the disposal of the country when their services are wanted for military purposes?

It is now.
Graduates of the Royal Military College pass immediately into the active militia and within two years have to become connected with some corps of the active militia in Canada. Immediately their names pass into the Militia List and are there recorded for service if required. That has always been the case. Recently we have added a regulation that within two years these cadets must connect themselves with some definite corps and we (also require them to attend two camps.

Young men are a little retarded in doing that, as they sometimes cannot get lieutenancies because the positions are occupied by other gentlemen.
I am not saying that these lieutenants should be removed, but if you want to get the services of your graduates you must devise some scheme of making vacancies without insulting somebody. My own son graduated last year. He has a good record for artillery 'and he wants to become lieutenant, but he cannot do so without asking for the resignation of some one else and that is something which no manly young man wants to do.
Under the rules to-day they can add a supernumerary to any battery.

Then, too, to-day we are giving a preference to graduates of the Royal Military College in our permanent force. Every month almost we are taking them on. Where there were two graduates of the Royal Military College in the permanent force of Canada fifteen years ago, I think there are seventy-five to-day, certainly seventy, in the employ of the Militia Department,
Does this resolution cover anything more than was covered by section 7?
It is an amendment of section 7 by eliminating the first part.
It does not say so.

It should.
* Mr. LENNOX, (reading):
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Royal Military College Act, chapter 43 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, by repealing section 7 and submitting therefor the following:-
7. The salaries, pay and allowances of the commandent and of the superior and subordinate staffs of the college shall be as fixed from time to time by the Governor in Council.
It is intended to leave the second part of that section.

The second part only provides that the detail of such salaries shall appear in the annual report laid before parliament. That is not what I wa3 directing my attention to more particularly. As far as the range of officers is concerned, it is intended to provide for the payment of the same class of persons.
Not necessarily the same. As the college grows, more professors are necessary. It is the same class, but not limited as to numbers.

Under the Act, the salary of the commandant shall not exceed $3,200 a year, and the others $30,000, so that, under section 7 of the Act, we have a limitation of the amount to $32,200. Now the minister suggests that we should make the limitation $60,000.
I understood the minister to say that he was already expending $51,000.
$51,500 is what we shall require this year.

That is a pretty big jump from $33,200. We have a statute in force which provides that the salaries shall not exceed $33,200, and yet we are spending actually $51,500. We have been voting this larger expenditure, but our attention was not called to the statute in any way. Although I quite recognize the necessity for a change, and do not want to limit the salaries to an unfair amount, still we have been exceeding the statutory limit.
I stated frankly that we had, as we supposed, obtained the authority of parliament for our expenditure, and no attempt was made to conceal the fact that the Act in question was on our statutes.
The minister's wording of this is incorrect.

Yes, whoever drafted the Bill made a mistake. There was no intention to repeal the second part. I quite agree to the limitation suggested. Perhaps on the whole it is desirable for the department, as well as parliament, that there should be a limitation, and I think that the amount of $60,000 will be satisfactory for many years to come.
The minister will still come down every year, and give the: specific amounts.
Certainly.

In case the Royal Military College were to be extended you would require a larger staff.

I would like to draw attention to this aspect of the case. These cadets have on various occasions given exhibitions of their skill in drill, &c., in Toronto and Montreal. I am sure it would only be a trifling expense, heartily endor-Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
sed by parliament to bring them to Ottawa, 30 that the members and senators, the people's representatives, could see what these young men are capable of in the way of physical training. I would be pleased if the minister would give the House the details of the studies and exercises of these cadets. He owes that to the country, and it would be a good advertisement of the institution.

The object of my hon. friend is all right, but it would be better attained by the members of parliament going to Kingston. I do not think it would be wise to bring a lot of cadets from their studies to exihibit themselves more or less as a circus for the benefit of members of parliament. The members of parliament ought to know how they live and what they are doing, and they could learn that a good deal better by going to Kingston. I would suggest that an arrangement should be made to take the members of parliament to Kingston on some Saturday, or several Saturdays, and there make themselves acquainted with the workings of the college.
I believe that it would be better that the members should go to the college, and learn there the work that is being done. I think that we ought to encourage members of parliament to see the college. Many members,
I believe, have a wrong impression of the benefits resulting from that institution, and if they went there, I think they would be agreeably surprised at the good work done.

Are officers brought out from England given a preference in appointments over graduates in the Royal Military College? I understand that to be the ease. It may be thought right to bring' English officers out here to give our young men sound ideas, but, if the college is doing its work properly, I do not see why we should not have in this country young men who are qualified to take their places alongside of any in the world. If there is to be a preference, I think the preference should be given to Canadians.

Before answering my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), I would like to say there is a great deal of merit in the suggestions made by both the hon. members who preceded him. I think it would be an excellent thing to have a visit from the Royal Military College cadets here, and I think it would be a better thing for hon. members to go to Kingston, and see the college.. So far as I am concerned, I shall do every-* thing in my power to further either of these ends. At this moment we are considering the question of having a visit from the college cadets in a short time. Something is going, on here, and I believe it is rather desirable that the cadets should

come. As to the other suggestion, I shall be glad to do what I can to arrange to have an excursion to visit the college, if any considerable number of members will make known their desire or their willingness to go.
Now, as to the selection of British officers, I am sure that my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) has no personal feelings against British officers.
None whatever.

I may tell the hon. member that the former commandant was a Royal Military College graduate. And, while I am not going to discuss his regime, I will say that we have had more successful commandants. At the present time there are two officers of the staff who are Royal Military College graduates. True, they are British officers, but it seems to me that in supplying teachers for the college, men are required who have had experience in military matters of the highest character, and that is the kind of men we try to get. The present commandant is a man of first-rate qualifications. I hope the day will come when, through a process of exchange which is now being carried on, between the permanent force officers of Canada and the British army, and the officers of the permanent forces of Australia and India, and other parts of the empire, we shall have in our own college our own officers who have had experience of service abroad to a sufficient extent to make them efficient teachers. At the present moment, I think the course we are following is decidedly the best one.

I was not referring- though I admit that there was nothing in my words to make that clear-to the higher officers such as the commandant, but to such officers as instructors. As an instance to illustrate what I mean, I may mention a gentleman by the name of Phillips, who, I am told, was brought out in 1909, as instructor of gunnery in Halifax. I understand that he took his qualifying course twelve years ago, and three years is supposed to he the period after which a man gets behind the times-I am not much of a military man, but that is what I am informed. Again, the officers who come here from England are granted two months leave of absence, while our own Canadians are granted only one month's leave. Yet these Canadians have passed the qualifying examinations of the Royal Military College, and I think we have a right to assume that those examinations are of a high enough standard to prove that the men have the qualifications to fill vacancies that occur from time to time. I am told that two of the graduating class wished to take commissions in the artillery-
This of which the hon. member is speaking, does not relate to the Royal Military College, I think.

These were graduates of the Royal Military College, and, in that respect, I think this pertains to the subject. I am told that two of the graduating class wished to take commissions in the artillery, and though there were, according to the militia list, five vacancies, only one position was given to a graduate of the college. If that sort of thing be true, it may be all Tight. I confess I am not a military man, but looking at it from the standpoint of a non-military man, I think it is not right.
Were these vacancies all filled?
I do not know.
They were not.
How many of them were filled?

I cannot say exactly; but I can say that, owing to not having sufficient and, perhaps, not really requiring officers at that particular time, these vacancies were not all filled. There are always vacancies in the permanent force-sometimes as many as fifteen. But I will look into the case to which the hon. member has referred. I am glad that he has brought it up. But, meantime, I may tell the hon. member that we give preference to graduates of the Royal Military College, if they are recommended by "the commandant over and above every other person and regardless of any consideration except that of merit.

I think that is very fair. I would ask the minister to look into the case of T. F. Grant. I believe he stood at the head of his class in the Royal Military College at Kingston, he came out at the top of the graduating class; and I am informed that he resigned as a protest against the advancement of an Englishman by the name of Ellison, who was brought out in 1906.

I remember the case. Ellison was. an English officer, who was stationed at Esquimalt, whc had had considerable experience, and he was appointed because we thought it was more in the interest of the public that he should be appointed. It is sometimes necessary for us to ask for the loan of an imperial officer, because at the moment we have not qualified officers of our own. We borrow these officers for a period, and if, at the end of that time, we have a Cana-

dian officer who is fit for the position, he gets it. I remember the case of a young Grant, and we are very sorry to lose him. I think he made a great mistake in going out.
Resolution reported, read the second time, and agreed to.
Sir FREDERICK BORDEN moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 180) to amend the Royal Military College Act.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

House went into. committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to authorize the Governor in Council: (a) To sell and dispose of the Baby farm, situate in the township of York, in the county of York, and province of Ontario, the acquisition of which was ratified by chapter 51 of the statutes of 1908. The purchase moneys received from the purchaser of the said land to he appropriated and used for the purchase of a site and the construction of barracks and buildings thereon for the housing of the militia and other military purposes in, or in the vicinity of, the city of Toronto, (b) To sell and dispose of that parcel of land situate in the municipality of As-siniboia, in the province of Manitoba, and now used and known as the Winnipeg rifle range. The purchase moneys received from the purchaser of the said range to be appropriated and used for the purchase of land for a rifle range in, or in the vicinity of, the city of Winnipeg, in the province of Manitoba.

Two years ago a Bill was passed by this House of a similar character, by which the government was enabled to sell certain properties, one in the city of Montreal and one in the city of Toronto, and utilize the proceeds for military purposes as stated in that Bill. This resolution proposes the sale of a property owned by the Militia Department, in or near the city of Toronto, known as the Baby farm. There are several reasons why we wish to sell this property. One is that it is not quite large enough. We are establishing in Toronto a new depot for the permanent force, and we want to have that depot advantageously situated. This farm was purchased for $20,000, it contains 160 acres, and we can sell it to-day for $160,000. So the country will have a very fair profit. I do not think it wise to state exactly where the property is situated which we propose to purchase, but it is situated near the city of Toronto, and in a position even more favourable than that of the Baby farm. It is very accessible, and in every way advantageous. It is proposed to acquire that property by expropriation, and steps will be taken to do that as soon as this legislation is assented to.
Where will it be?

I would rather not state that, because I am afraid the price of land might go up in that locality. But I have had the country examined all around adjacent to Toronto, and a very suitable place has been found.
What is the estimated cost?
It is expected that we can buy the property we want for about one-third the price that we will get for this property. It will contain from 300 to 600 acres.
If vou are going to expropriate it, why do you decline to tell us wrhere it is?
I think it is undesirable, even in that case.
I suppose the government will sell this property privately, for any price they choose?
No, we will ask for bids. We will advertise it for sale, but probably we will not sell it by public auction.
Has the minister had any valuations made of it? Because $1,000 an acre is not a very large price for land in the suburbs of Toronto.
We bought this property less than four years ago for $20,000. There are no buildings very near it.
Will the hon. gentleman have a valuation made, and fix a reserve bid?
Certainly, we propose to sell it openly.
Do I understand the minister to say that all the moneys received from the sale of these lands will be used in building?

Yes, every dollar.
On paragraph (b),

The same thing is true of the second part. The rifle range at Winnipeg is rather near the city, and we have not land enough there. With the strength of the modern up to date cartridges, the danger area is very much greater than it used to be, and we have been notified that it will be necessary to buy more land. We find that to buy land adjacent to the rifle range would cost as much as it will cost if we sell this land, go a little farther out of the city and buy about three. times the amount of land, which will enable us to have a rifle range there and to move our depot if we choose,

from the city of Winnipeg, which we will have to do in the near future. It will not cost the country a dollar, and it will be as convenient as the present range is to-day, because it is on the same line of electric railway.
Have you a new site for the rifle range?
Yes, we have selected the land. I do not know that it has been made nublic yet.
Is it the policy of the department to sell or lease lands of the department which are not used?

If the military authorities report that these lands are never likely to be required, and a reasonable price can be secured, the policy would be to sell them, but the policy since I came into office has been to lease them on condition that the department can take them over at short notice.
Has the minister had under consideration the removal of the troops from St. Johns, Quebec, and the selling of some public buildings there?
No, that has been reported m the newspapers, but it has not been under consideration.
What will be done with the present Stanley barracks site?
The barracks have been sold to the city.

In regard to the leasing of the lands of the department, is that done openly after tender, or is there any competition for them, or does it just happen that any person who makes application and is esteemed satisfactory by the officers of the department is allowed to lease these lands?

That would depend. A good many leases have been given without competition because the lands were not believed to be valuable. I usually leave that to the officer commanding. I believe there are some lands at Digby. I think the officer at Halifax would require to go there and make a report, and we would be guided very much by his report. We always put into the leases a provision that the department can take possession, without having to pay for buildings or improvements, at any time it sees fit, for military purposes.
Resolution reported, read the second time, and agreed to.
Sir FREDERICK BORDEN moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 181) to authorize the sale or other disposal of certain public lands, and the acquisition of certain other lands in or in the vicinity of
the cities of Toronto and Winnipeg, respectively.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
