House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to enable the Governor in Council to authorize the expenditure of a sum not exceeding fifty thousand dollars for investigating the processes used in the production of zinc, for making experiments, and for any other purpose that may be deemed advisable for the promotion of the production and manufacture in Canada of zinc and zinc products from Canadian ores.- Mr. Templeman.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The Bill which will be introduced on the passage of this resolution will provide for the diversion of $50,000 from the fund for present lead-bounty fund, for the purposes stated in the resolution. About $2,500,000 was voted several years ago for a bounty on lead and about $1,000,000 of that is still in the treasury. Lead and zinc are so closely allied, particularly in the ores in British Columbia, that the lead miners are deeply interested in the handling of the zinc product, and this proposal has the approval of all the lead mining interests. Upon a petition presented to the government and backed up by the lead mining interests, this step has been deemed advisable. The money is to be expended under the control of the Department of Mines. There are numerous metallurgical difficulties connected with the smelting of zinc. The presence of zinc is a detriment to the lead ores, and in this country the zinc product is absolutely lost under the present system of smelting, although zinc is the more valuable mineral of the two, quantity for quantity. It is proposed to investigate all known methods of electrical smelting of zinc. There are at present in Europe some new processes, one has been in use for years and the others are comparatively new, so that it is not known whether these are commercially successful or not. There have been two attempts at zinc smelting in British Columbia, one the well known process of smelting in retorts, and the other an electric process whereby it was hoped by the one operation to separate the lead and zinc in smelting, getting from the smelter the lead bullion and zinc bullion. That smelter was carried on experimentally for several years, but only with measurable success. The desire of the min-

ing men of the Kootenay is that the Department of Mines should carry to completion the experimentation that has gone on thus far in the zinc smelter at Nelson. After a thorough investigation of all well knowm processes, the one which is best adapted to the condition of Canadian ores will be adopted. I believe the object to be a very laudable one.

How will these investigations be carried on?
_ Mr. TEMPLEMAN. We hope that the investigations in Europe will be carried on by Mr. Harbord, a mining engineer of the city of London, who was on the commission which this government sent to Europe some years ago, and who is now employed investigating for the British government in South Africa. We have been in communication with this gentleman, and we hope to secure his services. The investigations in this country will be under Dr. Haanel, who will no doubt obtain the services of the best metallurgists he can in this country or elsewhere.
Where will the experiments he carried on?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: If we come to the conclusion that the electrical process may be applied to the refractory low grade ores of British Columbia, the further experiments will in all probability be carried out at Nelson, British Columbia, where an electric smelter with all the necessary equipment, as well as the electrical power, has been offered to us free of charge, for the purpose of experimentation. I assume that these experiments will be carried on at Nelson, although we want to have a free hand to carry them on in the city of Ottawa, or at any well equipped laboratory of a university, if we deem it wise to do so.
Has Dr. Haanel made any success of the experiments in smelting iron by electricity?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The smelting of iron by electricity is an accomplished fact.
But there has been no practical application of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Oh yes, it is carried on in Europe to a considerable extent, and to some extent in the United States, but its application is more to the manufacture of steel than of iron. The chief problem in electric smelting in this country is to get cheap electricity. If electricity can be produced cheaper than heat can be generated by the ordinary process there is no question at all but that electricity will quickly supersede the ordinary process of smelting iron.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue

speechtext: In view of the extensive water-powers in British Columbia you ought to have the cheapest electricity in the world.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We have also large deposits of coal in British Columbia, but strange to say electrical power is not quite so cheap in British Columbia at present as it is in Ontario. British Columbia is an enormous country in extent, and some of the water-powers are not contiguous to the iron. Progress has been made in the electrical smelting of iron, but I do not think Canada has taken advantage of the knowledge obtained along that line. Of course, the development of iron mines and the smelting of iron involves the expenditure of millions of capital.
Will any portion of this grant be used to send a commission to the old country to make an examination of conditions there?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: This matter has been under consideration for some considerable time, but it is not the intention of the department to send any one to Europe. There are metallurgical engineers fully conversant with the industry whose services can be obtained at comparatively little cost. We will obtain the latest information as to the development that has taken place in the smelting of zinc ore, but it will not be necessary to send a commission to Europe. The necessity is more apparent now than it was a few years ago. Formerly, zinc ores went to the United States from Canada at a comparatively low duty, but under the Payne-Aldrich tariff the duty was made prohibitive. ' Hence the necessity to provide some method of handling m this country these zinc products. This money is being diverted from the lead bounty. The beneficiaries of the lead bounty are practically the beneficiaries of this, as lead and zinc go hand in hand, zinc being a great detriment to the lead men, and absolute waste at present, so that all those, whj profit by the lead bounty have virtually asked the government to take $50,000 off it and carry on the -work of experimenting in zinc production and manufacture.

As I understand the ore formerly went to the United States and was smelted there, with every satisfaction to the producers of zinc ore m British Columbia, this $50,000 is practically a bonus to a smelter in that western country. Is not that the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Of course it is not, as my hon. friend will see if he reads the resolution. Only a comparatively small quantity of zinc ore ever went from British Columbia to the United States. There is a vast quantity of low grade ore -which cannot be concentrated sufficiently to pay the

cost of transportation, and we propose to devote thi3 money to the purpose mentioned in the resolution, and no other. We could not possibly give one dollar of it to subsidize a smelter in British Columbia. It will take several years to expend the money, and the entire amount will be spent by the Department of Mines in carrying out the objects of the resolution.

The last clause distinctly says ' and for any other purpose that may be deemed advisable for the promotion of the production and manufacture in Canada of zinc and zinc products from Canadian ores/ Would not that justify the inference I have made?
What does the minister aim at in using the language my hon. friend 'has just quoted?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We aim, in the first place, at a full investigation of the known electrical processes of smelting zinc. We aim at a full examination into the zinc and zinc products in Canada. We aim also at a full examination of the known deposits in Canada to ascertain what tonnage we could have to keep a smelter running. In addition, we aim at carrying on experiments by the department, under properly qualified men, if we can get them-and there are not so many-who have a knowledge of the electrical processes of smelting zinc, and we expect to- carry on that experimentation in Nelson, where a smelter already exists, the use of which has been offered the department for that purpose. It may be necessary to ask some of the metallurgists of the School of Mines in Kingston or at other places to carry on certain experimentations in order to ascertain whether it is possible for them to separate lead and zinc at one process, and it may be necessary for them to call in tfie assistance of other experts. [DOT]
The hon. minister should then have no objection to strike out the words ' and for any other purpose.'

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not know what effect that would have. I want to have the fullest liberty and authority to spend the money for the purposes I have named. There is no intention to bonus any zinc smelter, and you could not possibly bonus one with this sum. We have no objection to prohibiting the use of any of this money for bonuses for any zinc industry, for that is not contemplated.

Has the hon. minister received any intimation of a discovery of zinc ore m the counties of Grey and Bruce, Ontario? I have had some letters on that subject, and I understand they have a very good sample of zinc, but they want some assistance in working the prospect out. Is it the intention of the minister to give any such assistance?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The very thing that the Department of Mines is trying to do is to afford assistance to the mining industry, but not financial assistance. We attempt work of research, experimentation and publication; we try to show the way in which things are to be done, that the mining interests may take advantage of the information placed at their disposal to develop our mineral resources. I am aware that there are considerable zinc deposits in Ontario, and have had some letters on the subject since this resolution was placed on the order paper; but in the case of the zinc industry in Ontario, as well as m British Columbia, we can only assist by showing the way-that is, if we can manage to solve the questions ourselves. But the problem is one in which we cannot be sure of success altogether. When you take up the question of electric smelting, you are up against considerable difficulties. I think it most likely that we shall require all this money for the purpose contemplated, 1 can assure the House, and my hon. friends opposite, that I do not desire to change the wording. The Bill which will be submitted to the House on the passage of this resolution, was prepared by the Deputy Minister of Justice, and the notice on the order paper was prepared by the law clerk, The notice practically follows the wording of the Bill. But, not being a lawyer, I am rather chary of giving consent to striking out words when such a change, though, apparently, innocent enough, may have the effect of rendering the Bill nugatory.

But the point is that the minister is going to place his smelter in British Columbia, where it can hardly be expected to treat the ores of Ontario. And I have understood that it is too expensive to send this ore for treatment to the United States. If the smelter had been more centrally placed, I think the minister's position in this matter would be much stronger.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Of course, the question of where the smelter is to be placed is purely an economic problem. A smelter for zinc ores, or for any other ores, must be so placed that power will cost, as little as passible. It may be possible to haul the ore a long distance where you get cheap power. One of our serious problems, in western Canada at all events, is to combine all the conditions. One of the great difficulties in British Columbia was that the cost of operating the Frank smelter was too great, although there were other defects. That may be found to be the case with electric smelting also. But the conditions must be learned. In the smelting of iron, it is sometimes cheaper to take the iron to the coal than the coal to the iron.

I am glad the minister 1 mentioned the subject of cheap power, for,

that being so important, I think he will find that the city of London is the best place for the smelter. We have excellent conditions there, and we expect to have the Niagara power at very cheap rates. Of course, I cannot vouch for that. But I do not know of a better place thon London for such an industry, and I trust he will take it into his careful consideration.

We do not wish to embarrass the minister by urging him to strike out words, for I can well understand that sometimes it is difficult to know just what the effect of striking out words will be. However, the minister can probably obviate that by giving us information which we are entitled to have, and which he has no doubt at his fingers' ends. I understood him to say that he would require the whole of this $50,000 for the purposes indicated.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Lennox) is pausing for an answer. That means ' yes ' or ' no.' I said I had no doubt that this money would be needed. If we are going into experiments in electrical smelting, it is very difficult to estimate how much money may be expended. Frankly, I admit that this whole $50,000 may be expended, and no positive results in regard to electric smelting may be obtained. The House ought to understand that. But, on the other hand, we might hit upon a plan of smelting before we had exhausted the $50,000. So, I do not say absolutely that we shall require all this money, but I believe the probabilities are that ive shall require it, and more.

The minister, I think, has hardly treated us fairly. When he comes to ask for $50,000, he does not ask it for pocket money, to spend or not to spend as may happen; he is asking for something which he knows he will want, in other words, he has some plan, some estimate, showing how the money is expected to be applied. He says he wants $50,000 for experimental purposes. Well, we have the right to know, and, of course, he wants to tell us, to what purposes he proposes to apply the money. If he does not know, even in a general way, to what purposes he intends to apply it, he has no right to ask for it, and we have no right to grant it. What I ask the minister to do is to give us the various items of this proposed expenditure. We shall then be in a position to judge whether it is our duty to join with him in the appropriation of this money, or whether we should oppose him in it. I have stated this in support of his plea against striking out words m this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
There is an estimate, but I did not suppose it would be required at this stage, and did not bring it Mr. BEATTIE.
with me. This is merely the introductory resolution. If my hon. friend will accept the explanation he asks for on the second reading of the Bill, I shall be glad to give it then.
I take the minister's word, and am quite willing that the course he proposes should be taken.

I am aware of the difficulties that have been met in finding methods for the treatment of zinc ores.
I feel inclined to agree with the minister, particularly as I understand that a portion of this money will be taken from the grant already passed by parliament for treating lead ores. That grant has proved very beneficial not only to this particular industry but to the Dominion as a whole. Heretofore all the lead for paints ground in oil were imported from the United States; but, I am glad to say, that we have very large works of this kind established in Montreal, so that a large portion of the lead used in Canada is mined, smelted, ground and manufactured in the Dominion. As to zinc ores, I can speak with some little knowledge, because our own government has expended a good deal of money trying, to discover an electric process of treating these ores. One of our difficulties is that, owing to the action of the United States, we have found it difficult to market the lead ores containing zinc. Particular ores containing a certain percentage of zinc are practically prohibited by the duties, so we are unable to take out the slocan ore which contains a large percentage of zinc. The result is that many of the mines have been closed down, and many others have large dumps of second-class ore containing zinc in their composition, but as they cannot be treated in any way they are now comparatively a waste product. If by assistance from the government we can devise a process whereby these ores can be treated, it would be of great benefit to the whole Dominion, and a great stimulus to the production of zinc in our own country. On that ground I will support the proposition of the minister. I may add from my experience of this question that it is difficult to say just how much experiments of that kind would cost. We have spent large sums of money, many of us have lost money in trying to discover successful processes; and the feeling is that as the project is a benefit to the whole people of Canada, it is a subject of fair consideration by the government. It is on that ground ' that representations were made to the minister asking a grant of this nature. These experiments cest a lot of money, and sometimes produce little results, but we have to do these things if we are going to develop mining in our country. We were

the first country to adopt the electrocly-tic process in the refining of lead, and the result is that we are now doubling the capacity of one of the largest smelters on the American continent, and we are turning out the purest lead produced on the American continent. I have thought it well to give these few facts to the House in order to induce the House to support the minister in the object be has in view.

I sympathize with the view presented by the hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve). But what I desire to say to the minister is that when he comes and asks us for money he should be able to set forth a method by which he proposes to spend the money. I will be prepared to join in expending far more than $50,000 for the development of mining. But when the minister asks us for money I ask him to tell us how he proposes to spend it. I do not know anything about this particular grant of money, but I regard $50,000 for the purpose of developing any useful industry as a very small sum of money. I will be glad to assist the minister in getting a larger sum of money so long as the plan he outlines to parliament seems calculated to benefit the country. I could apply in this case that hackneyed expression so often used in railroading Bills through this House, that the development of mining in British Columbia, or anywhere else in Canada, is a work for the general advantage of Canada. I am heartily in accord with any proposition for the development of mining, and I hope the minister will bring down information to show us that this money is going to be wisely expended.

I desire to ask the minister if the government has done anything towards investigating the zinc smelter enterprise in the town of Frank. It was to some extent a failure when first established. It is a very extensive plant.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The government has not investigated the zinc smelting industry in the town of Frank, but I think that mining men of the country generally have investigated it. It was a failure, probably built on the wrong lines to smelt the zinc ores of the Kootenay country. At all events, it was a metallurgical and financial failure, and if I am not mistaken the plant has been dismantled.
Resolution reported, read the second time, and agreed to.
Mr. TEMPLEMAN moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 182) respecting the payment of bounties on lead contained in leadbearing ores mined in Canada, and to promote the production in Canada of zinc.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

What do you mean by the yrords 'loathsome disease'?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The disease which is most frequently met with is trachoma, which is rather loathsome than dangerous.
The word ' loathsome ' as used there simply expresses the condition of the nervous system of the person who is looking at the disease. A medical man would not consider any disease loathsome.
What word would the hon. gentleman suggest in lieu .of ' loathsome '?
It is not necessary at all; the words contagious and infectious are sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: While there may be no scientific warrant for the use of the word I think it will be found very desirable to retain it for the purpose of administering the Act.
There are diseases which are neither contagious nor infectious, but which are loathsome, such as cancer and ulcers. I do not think you could select a better word.
I do not think trachoma would be loathsome in the eyes of a medical man. From a medical point of view there is not any such thing as disgusting or loathsome disease.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In connection with this section I might say that it has been urged that it is too restrictive in that it purports to restrict the landing of persons to whom money has been loaned. If the restriction were confined to loans by charitable organizations, it would probably meet all necessary requirements. Loans advanced by a friend should not come under this prohibition.
What is the distinction?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A loan that is given by pne friend to another is a different thing from a loan given by a charitable organization in carrying out the purposes of the organization.

I do not think that persons should be excluded simply because they borrow money. It is quite sufficient to restrict those who are sent out here by charitable organizations who may wish to get rid of them.

Eecently a number of Scotchmen landed in Canada who had not Mr. OLIVEE.
sufficient money to comply with the requirements of the Act, and the money was furnished by a Scottish society. What position would these men be in under this Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That was not a loan by a charitable organization for the purpose of sending out these immigrants.
And it was given after they landed in Canada.
I do not think it would be right to make a restriction that would shut out such persons who were aided by their compatriots in this country.

As a matter of fact quite a number of immigrants secure passage from the steamship companies to the ocean port in Canada, and they may want to go to Toronto or Winnipeg, or some western point, but have not sufficient money, although they may be otherwise desirable immigrants. The steamship agent will say to them, you have plenty of money to go to Halifax or St. John, and we will give you passage, and these people assume that once they land in Canada, they will have no difficulty in reaching any place to which they intend going. Frequently families of that kind, good people, have come to Canada, and have been assisted by our national societies. We have in Halifax three such societies, the Charitable Irish Society, the North British Society, and the St. George's Society, organized principally for the purpose of assisting such needy immigrants, their own compatriots. There was a case the other day to which my hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) has just referred. The North British Society took that case up and furnished those people with sufficient money to get to their destination. There is no doubt that they were people of very creditable character as immigrants, and it would have been a great hardship had they been turned back, and, under the strict letter of the law, they would have had to be deported. I think that the Lieutenant Governor of Nova Scotia interested himself in their behalf. There should be some provision to enable such immigrants to get to their destination. I think there is a case of the kind now in St. John, of a man who has been there some eight or ten days. His brother-in-law, who is a well-to-do citizen in Toronto, wired sufficient money to qualify him, but there is this difficulty, that, according to the strict letter of the law, he should be deported. I am sure that the minister must have had many demands made on him in regard to the character of immigrants. When a man is of good character, and shows cause why he should not be deported, and has friends, as sometimes happens, who are prepared to help him there should be some way of preventing his being deported as an undesirable immigrant.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This section, as it stands, represents the position which the government take to-day, and which it enforces under orders in council, which are authorized by the present Act. It was with the desire to place upon the statute the' policy of the government, so that whatever might be done would be done in the light of day, that we proposed this section. I quite appreciate the fact that many a good man is poor, and that, Jf poverty were a bar to admission into this country, many of us would have been excluded, but this provision was rendered necessary by the conditions which arose in the fall of 1907, and which would very likely arise again if it were not enforced. Everybody will remember that in the winter of 1907, there was a great deal of distress in many cities of Canada among newly arrived immigrants, and the Immigration Department was subjected to a great deal of very severe criticism in consequence. We found that the large majority of these cases arose as the result of the efforts of charitable organizations operating on the other side. There had been a good demand for labour in Canada during the summer, and there was considerable dearth of employment in the old country. The charitable organizations there spent in consequence considerable money in sending out their unemployed to Canada, where employment was found for them during the summer months; but as soon as employment began to slacken in the fall of 1907, we had this large number of people on our hands, and had nothing for them to do. A great deal of distress resulted, and a great deal of harsh criticism on the Immigration Department, and the cause of legitimate immigration to Canada was seriously injured'in England by the reports that went back of this distress. An order in council was then passed prohibiting people, who had been assisted by charitable organizations, from landing in this country, unless before sailing they had passed inspection, and been approved by our immigration officers. I am quite aware that cases of hardship arise, and would be very glad if we could find some means of avoiding these cases, but that does not seem possible. We found the provision we made by order in council not only necessary, but useful. I believe it absolutely saved the situation in Canada, and I would like to see that provision embodied in this Act so that all the world would see exactly what our policy is.
WTould this provision interfere in any^ way with the measures which the Salvation army has been taking lately in the way of aiding immigration to this country?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Salvation army complies with this requirement. They always
have the people in whom they are interesting themselves pass inspection in the old country before our immigration officers; and of course, once they pass that inspection, we become responsible for the character, and standing of these immigrants, and they are allowed to enter at our ports. Some other charitable organizations comply with that provision also. We do not forbid the bringing in of people by charitable organizations, but they must first pass an inspection on the other side by our officers.
I think that is very proper.

We have in Halifax three incorporated societies, not exclusively charitable, but national as well, which assist people of their nationality who come to this country. Very often when a family of such people land in Halifax or St. John, they imagine that they are close to every place in Canada. Take the case of a family of Irish people coming to this country, intending to go to Toronto or Winnipeg to join friends, but without the necessary money. We have frequently supplied the funds to take these people to their destination, and in many cases have afterwards received the money back from them. None of these incorporated societies would take hold of a family, and forward them to their destination without being reasonably sure that they were suitable immigrants for this country. The Charitable Irish Society, and the North British Society were established a hundred and fifty years ago to help immigrants coming to this side-sometimes they have received people who were shipwrecked on the coast of Nova Scotia, and sent them forward to their destinations. I think that these societies would be perfectly willing to give any reasonable guarantee in the case of the people they assist. But some regulation should be incorporated in the Bill to provide foT cases of this kind so that desirable immigrants may not be deported.

I think there is something in what the hon. member for Halifax has just stated. I have known of cases of hardship in my own riding It sometimes happens that people having a father or brother coming from the old country are not in a position to supply the $25 referred to, but they were ready to put up bonds that, if these people should ever become a public burden, they would undertake to send them back. Yet, in the face of that, these immigrants have been deported to the great regret of their friends. Such cases are certainly cases of hardship. It seems to me, however, that the only way in which we can meet them is by tire appointment of intelligent agents, and giving

these agents some little latitude to discriminate between the desirable and undesirable.

We are getting a little ahead of the Bill. I think that under section 13, providing for a board of inquiry where an immigrant has been rejected, the minister has made provision to meet such cases. We can discuss the_ matter more understandingly on that section.
If this section be amended by making it refer to assistance by a charitable organization, should it not be made clear that it applies to charitable organizations in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This section applies only to organizations outside of Canada,. It provides that, in the case of parties aided by charitable organizations, they must be inspected and approved by our officers on the other side of the water, or we do not allow them to land here. We assume that a charity-aided immigrant is an undesirable immigrant, and the burden of proof of the contrary is on him. We provide means for trying out cases on the other side of the water. With regard to what my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Crosby) has said, I may explain that if the people are of the class and character suitable for farm work, we do not require them to have any money in possession, we only require that they should be able to reach their work.
How about domestic servants?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are in the same position as farm help. Everybody recognizes that there is need of farm labour and domestic service, and we impose no restriction as to money qualifications in these cases. But there is a clear distinction between these and other classes who come, and we think that when people come in to engage in other callings it is right that there should be a proper safeguard that they will not become a public burden.
What classes does the government bonus now?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Farmers, farm labour, and domestic service.
Have you dropped the railway navies?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, over a year ago.
Would fraternal or national societies come under this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly, if they are on the other side of the water.
I know some such societies on this side that contemplate bringing out immigrants, selecting desirable ones.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no objection whatever, provided their efforts are directed to securing farmers, farm assistants or domestic help.
And people of these classes are not required to have the $25 on landing?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
Nor do you take a bond from the society that they shall not become a public burden?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. We know that there is such a demand for this class of people, that, if they are sound physically and of reasonably good disposition, there is no question as to their getting employment.

The clause as amended should be acceptable to the House. We have been trying for years to have only a desirable class of immigrants come into this country, and I think we might reasonably go a little too far in that direction rather than stop short. It is most desirable to keep up the standards of our people.

A case arose in the town of Trail, which is next to my own town. Some Italians communicated with me with regard to some of their friends coming out from Italy. These people landed in New York. Some had bought their tickets through to British Columbia, while others had bought only to New York. They were held by the agent there. A number of telegrams passed between myself and Mr. Scott, the commissioner of immigration. I learned that all these immigrants got through except one, and as to that one I did not get any definite answer. I may say that one of the men who communicated with me on the subject was an expert metallurgist, a man in good position. I desire to ask the minister on what ground people would be refused admission under the circumstances to which I have referred?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That was under a short amendment of the Immigration Act that was passed in the session before last, what is called the indirect passage provision. It provides that we may exclude immigrants who come otherwise than by direct passage, or on a through ticket purchased in the country of which they are citizens. I suppose I may mention the reasons for this somewhat peculiar provision. The necessity arises from the exigencies of deportation. If an undesirable arrives and is rejected after he has been in the country for some time, we-then call unon the transportation company which brought him here to take him back to the country to which he belongs. But, if the transportation company which brought him into Canada did not bring him from the coun-

try to which he belongs, then we cannot compel them to take him hack to that country. We can only compel them to take him back to the country they brought him from, and if he was an undesirable in our country he may be just as undesirable in that country. So in order to secure ourselves we had this amendment passed, which gave us a right to exclude passengers who arrive otherwise than by direct passage or on through tickets purchased in the country in which they were citizens. That is the general statement. The particular condition was that there was a prospect, in fact a certainty, of a large movement of Japanese from Honolulu to British Columbia, and there was also the prospect of a large movement of Hindus from Hong Kong. We had an arrangement -with Japan whereby Japan prohibited emigration direct from that country to Canada, but Japan had no authority to prohibit emigration from the 'Sandwich Islands to Canada, they being part of the United States. There were a good many thousands of Japanese in those islands, where times were dull, and -prospects were good in British Columbia. There was every prospect of a large movement, and we successfully adopted this means of preventing that movement. The same provision applied to the movement that we apprehended from Hong Kong, and it also had the same effect. Of course it is a general provision, and is just as necessary and suitable in the case of undesirables coming through the United States as in any other case.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the case of immigrants who enter our ports with through tickets to the United States. They are carried through the Dominion as far as Sarnia, we will say, to the port of entry into the United States. I have knowledge of a case of that kind, where some 30 immigrants, who apparently had tickets to the United States, were turned back at the port of entry at Port Huron. Those men were placed on the Grand Trunk train and brought back to London, Ontario. So far as I could gather they were employed in London by the agents of the Grand Trunk railway, and in some other districts where they wished to make use of them; they were sent up into those districts to work. Now, if these immigrants were not fit for entrance into the United States, why should we be burdened with them in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not understand how that occurrence could take place if there was fair play on the part of all parties concerned. Every immigrant who lands at a Canadian port destined tor the United 184
States is examined at the Canadian port of landing by a United States officer, under a tacit arrangement between the two departments. When the United 'States officer at the Canadian ocean port has examined an immigrant and approved him, the immigrant is then free to enter the United States when he reaches the border. If the examination made by the United States officer at the port of Halifax, St. John or Quebec, is not effective in allowing the immigrant to pass into the United States when he reaches the border, I shall be glad to be informed of the circumstances. and we will have the situation readjusted.

I hone the minister will investigate that circumstance, because hundreds are turned back in the same manner. Personally I made inquiries about these people, having noticed them in Sarnia, and riding back to London in another car. They were taken off there, and I made some inquiries as to what was going to be done with them, and I received the information I have given to the minister. I am satisfied from what I can learn from the residents in our western country, that not only at the port of entry of Port Huron, but at other ports, many immigrants who have passages paid through to the United States are turned back at the border.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If my hon. friend has the particulars in regard to this case I would be glad to get them from him, or of any similar case hereafter that comes to his notice. Such a proceeding as he mentions is entirely contrary to our arrangement and understanding. I may say that our requirements in regard to the standard of immigrants are somewnat higher than the requirements of the United States, consequently there is a possibility of immigrants taking advantage of the more lenient law's of the United States in order to get into Canada; that is to say, ostensibly they are going through, but really they never intend to go through, and take advantage of the examination of the United States officers at the Canadian port in order to get into Canada. That is a very difficult situation, and one of the purposes of the Bill is to meet it as well as it can be met. We have certain provisions further on in the Bill which will go as far as we think it is possible to go in meeting that condition.
Has the minister certain officers in England for the purpose of bringing out immigrants to the province of Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
Has he not a gentleman by the name of Burnett in his department, and what is he doing?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is a salaried a'gent resident in York. We have no agents in England or on the continent who are conducting parties of immigrants to Canada.
Are his functions to send immigrants to Ontario or to the Northwest?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To any part of Canada that the immigrant desires to go. He is not to give anybody advice, but to give all the information he possesses.

This officer has been receiving letters from people who desired to come to this country. A man and his sons were sought to be induced to come to Canada to go to work as hired men. I think these people should be told that hired men only get employment for a few months in the year. To my mind that is one of the most serious things in connection with this business, that these men are rushed into the country under great inducements to work as harvesters when the work only lasts a short time. There should be some settled policy on the part of the government in this matter, whereby the immigration officers should show these people plainly and frankly when they come out as hired men what they have to expect. Whether they come out as labourers or as homesteaders, they should have all the facts placed before them; this family comes from near Carlisle. A young man who wrote me in Africa; I knew him very well. Burnett recommended this man with his family to come out here and hire on a farm in Ontario. I do not think there is any future for an ordinary man coming out here with a family to depend on a few months work only in each year.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not altogether agree with my hon. friend. The business of our agent there is to give information in regard to all parts of Canada, and the immigrant then makes his own choice as to where he wishes to go. It might not suit some men to go to the Northwest to take up farms, and it might suit them, if they so please, to seek employment at farm labour in Ontario. I am aware that there is at the present time a very strong demand for farm labour in Ontario.
For the summer.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And in the dairying districts for the winter as well.
And then these fellows hang around the towns in the winter.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Very true.

Oshawa is an instance of it.	.
Mr. OLIVER

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am well aware of that. 1 do not think it would be taken very kindly by the people of Ontario if we made a business of advising men who might be desirous of entering upon farm labour not to go to Ontario. There are, I think, every year cheap excursions from Ontario to the west for the harvest season, and it seems to me that the fact that a man goes to Ontario to take employment there is no guarantee that he is not going west to take a free farm in due course. I do not find any fault with our agent in giving this man and his son such information as they desired, and which led them to go to Ontario.
They have not gone; I am sending them to Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I hope they will do well in Alberta.

I intend to move a couple of amendments to this sectipn and I think that probably the minister will find that he will be able to adopt them, but before I do so I wish to say that I have no desire to be understood as obstructing this measure. There is an editorial in the Ottawa ' Free Press ', of to-day, the last paragraph of which reads as follows :
Should the obstruction continue the opposition must not complain if the suspicion gains ground that they are influenced by the shipping interests who are known to oppose the proposed new immigration regulations.
I presume this alludes to the discussion which took place when the hon. Minister of the Interior moved the second reading of this measure some days ago. Upon that occasion I was one of those who spoke. I spoke very briefly as did other members interested in this measure, and we did not take up any great amount of time. I do not think that three hours discussion on the second reading of an important measure of this character should be construed as obstruction, and I sincerely hope that this editorial paragraph which I have read was not in any way inspired by any member of the government. It would seem to me that when an important measure of this character is brought down it is not only the privilege of every member of this House to offer such suggestions a3 he believes to be in the public interest, but it is the duty of every man who is interested in the Bill to make such suggestions as in his opinion will advance the well being of the country, and the observations that were offered by myself, and other hon. gentlemen on that occasion were entirely along that line. I wish to say a word with regard to paragraph (a) of section 3, which has reference to prohibited classes. It reads:
(a) Idiots, imbeciles, feeble-minded persons, epileptics, insane persons and persons who have been insane within five years previous.

Shall be excluded. I wish to move an amendment that:
The word ' previous ' be stricken out and that in lieu thereof there shall be inserted the words ' who had two or more attacks of insanity previously/
I find that the American Act is very much along the lines, so far as prohibited classes are concerned, of this Act, and it seems to me that that would be a very proper addition to make to that section. There can be nothing objectionable in it. At a later stage I wish to move another amendment to section (d).

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would very much prefer that my hon. friend would not press his amendment. I am quite aware that it is contained in the United States Act, and while we have taken advantage of a good deal of the work that has been done in the drafting of the United States Act we have not found it advantageous to follow it in all particulars. The reason we do not follow it in this particular is that we desire to have the Act as clear as possible, so that it can be administered fairly to all parties. We think that if the prohibition with regard to insanity is fixed at a period of five years it is within a period that i3 capable of demonstration and proof on one side, or the other, whereas, if we accept the amendment that my hon. friend has suggested, and which speaks of two periods of insanity at any time in a person's life, there arises a difficulty in regard to the evidence on one side or the other that renders very difficult the administration of the law. I do not think it is really necessary that the provision should be such as my hon. friend has suggested, and I know that it would render the provision very much more difficult of fair administration. The great purpose we have in bringing in this Act before the House, and the country is that we may have something which will appeal to everybody as setting out a certain policy and as providing for a fair administration oi that policy, an administration that everybody will understand, and that everybody will have a fair chance under, leaving as little as possible to the uncertainty of the law. For that reason I ask my hon. friend not to press his amendment.	'

I do not see the difficulty of the minister. What the mover of the amendment asks is that a man who has been insane within five years of his attempt to enter into this Dominion shall be excluded. The word ' previous ' is absolutely needless. It cannot refer to the future; it must be in the past. A man who within five years from the time of his coming to this country has been insane should be excluded. The minister admits that, and therefore it is unnecessary to put in the word ' previous '. The proposed amend-1841
ment is this: ' or who had two or more attacks of insanity previously '. My hon. friend from Digby does not limit himself to a man who within five years has been insane, but if at any time during that man's life he can be proved to have been twice insane he shall be excluded. I cannot understand the objection to it.
Amendment negatived.

I would propose an amendment to subsection (d) which reads:
Persons who have been convicted of any crime involving moral turpitude.
I hope the minister will adopt this suggestion because I think it is along the lines he had in mind when drafting this Bill, although it seems to have been overlooked in this instance. Again, I have borrowed somewhat from the American Act and I propose, in substitution of this section, as follows:
Persons who have been convicted of a felony or other crime or misdemeanour involving moral turpitude, polygamists, anarchists, or persons who believe in or advocate the overthrow by force or violence of the government of Great Britain, of Canada, or other British colony, possession, or dependency, or any foreign government.	.
We have no need for such persons in this country, and they ought to be excluded. In section 41 the Bill provides for the removal |Or deportation from Canada of certain persons of this class, and it seems to me that if we are going to deport people-who exhibit tendencies of that character, it would be but the part of prudence to prevent them from entering Canada. My amendment is drawn with that idea in view. I can see good reasons why this amendment should canv, and I cannot see any reason why it should not. I move it, seconded bv Mr. Barker.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The law already in force in Canada is practically in the words of tire present Bill, and I believe that the provisions are satisfactory and sufficient. That provision of the United States Act has not had the slightest effect in preventing the entrance into the United States of any of these persons, because knowledge of the fact with regard to them in this respect can only be obtained by the confession of the person himself, and if he wants to come into the country he is not likely to make that admission.
Can you exclude a polygamist under the present Canadian law?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He can be deported.
Who pays the cost of the deportation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The transportation company who brought the person here. At

present we can deport him any time within tw(o years, but the Bill makes it three years, and the transportation company which carried him here must take him back.
But the government has expended money for deportations.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That was in cases where it was not possible to establish that the person arrived by a certain transportation company.
If the undesirable immigrant were bagged at the port without being allowed to land, you would get over that difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is true.

The minister uses the somewhat extraordinary argument that if an anarchist is admitted they will deport him, but. if they know he is coming in they will let him in and deport him afterwards.
Amendment (Mr. Jameson) negatived.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I move that the following be added as paragraph ' I.'
Persons who do not fulfil or comply with the conditions or requirements of any regulations which for the time being are in force and applicable to such persons under sections 37 or 38 of this Act.
The section provides that regulations shall be passed by the- Governor in Council with respect to persons mentioned in sections 37 and 38 as among the prohibited classes, and this puts it in the statute. I wish to put as much as we can on the face of the Act.

I think the regulations would be just as effective without this, but I believe in the principle of incorporating it in the statute.
. Amendment agreed to.
On section 4,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is a provision of the Australian Act. I need not enlarge on the difficulties of administering an immigrant exclusion provision. These provisons must be strong if they are to be of any value at all, and if we make them strong there necessarily will arise from time to time exceptional cases, so that without such a provision as this the law might work contrary to what is considered to be in the public interest. In Australia they found it desirable to give authority to the minister, who is responsible, to make an exception, and we have thought it would tend to perhaps do -away with instances of difficulties which would seem to discredit the drastic provisions of the Act if he had this power.
There will be a record of all such cases?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
On section 5,
The Governor in Council may appoint a superintendent of immigration, commissioners of immigration, and such other officers as are deemed necessary for ca'rrying out the provisions of this Act.
Is there any stipulated salary attached to each of these positions?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have a general scale of salaries, but no statutory provision.
Do these agents, who are employed at Ottawa, come under the Civil Service Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.
On section 10,
Every officer appointed under this Act shall have the authority and power of a special constable to enforce any of the provisions of this Act relating to the arrest, detention or deportation of [DOT] immigrants, aliens or other persons.
Why should a constable have the power to deport?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He has not the power to deport, but has authority to use force in restraining nr compelling detention or the movements of people under deportation.
On section 12,
Eor the preservation of the peace, and in order that arrests may be made for offences against the laws of Canada, or of any province or municipality thereof, wherein the various immigrant stations are located, the officers in charge of such immigrant stations, as occasion may require,, shall admit therein any constables or other peace officers charged with the enforcement of such laws; and for the purposes of this section the authority of such officers and the jurisdiction of the local courts shall extend over such immigrant stations.
Why do you want the word peace ' in line 6?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We borrow-ed this section from the United States Act, and have followed the very wording -of it.

I think it would be stronger without the word ' peace.'
On section 13,
The minister may appoint three or more officers, of whom the immigration officer in charge shall be one, at any port of entry, to act as a permanent Board of Inquiry for the summary determination of all cases of immigrants or passengers seeking to enter Canada or detained for any cause under this Act,
Where are the board of inquiry now established?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have power to establish them, and we propose to do so, and the object, is to do away with the arbitrary

methods of dealing with detention or deportation cases which prevails now. At present any action depends directly on the action of the superintendent, and we wish to have, as it were, courts of inquiry, the proceedings of which shall be of record.
How many do you.intend establishing?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We intend to have boards of inquiry at Halifax, St. John, Quebec and possibly at Montreal, and the principal ports on the Pacific coast.
What about the border points?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: By the following section we have the saqie provision with regard to border points. Where there are not sufficient officers to constitute a board, we give authority to the one officer there who shall keep a record.

I would like to know if the powers are to extend merely to investigation into the character of the immigrant and the mode of deportation and matters of the kind, or is it intended that the board is to have broader powers extending to the details of immigration generally? I think it would be worthy of consideration whether the board would be able to handle this matter better than having the work all in the hands of the minister, who is already overworked.

I am not sure, but that, under section 13, the minister is encumbering the procedure unnecessarily. He has an officer at the port of landing, and all these proceedings are taken only in the event of a dispute as to that officer's action. If the minister sends twro officers, in case of a protest against the port officers' ruling there may be a further dispute. If he were to send dowm one competent officer, and that officer agreed with the port officer, that should settle the matter. But, in case of difference, there could be such appeal as the minister provides.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Our object is to give the person who is the subject of detention an opportunity to present his case, to give him, so to speak, a fair trial, rather than, as at present, the department takes the responsibility of an arbitrary action without a form of trial.

It is clear that the minister is trying to afford the immigrant-an appeal. But-, in the case of a difference between the port officer, and the special officer of the department, why not have an appeal at once to the minister. You do not add anything to the advantage of the immigrant by sending two men. If you *send one officer, and there is a difference of opinion between him, and the port officer the immigrant would have an appeal to the department.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is true. Still, I should think that if there were a board of three, and two decided against the immigrant, he would be more apt to accept the decision of the two against one, than if it were a decision upon which the two differed.
Still more, if you made it four against five.

I would ask the minister to answer the question I mentioned a moment ago. Under the clause the operation of this board would extend merely to detention and deporting of immigrants. But has the minister taken into consideration the extension of the power of this board to the whole system, so that a board whose members shall devote their whole time to the work may deal with the whole range of immigration, thus relieving the minister of a great deal of work?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The provision of this Bill only looks to dealing with the administration of the Act at the port of landing. The suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Herron), goes very much further than that. We have not made any provision in the Act looking to that end.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: For the reasons I gave in a previous case I ask that the words 'and persons who have Canadian domicile' be inserted after the word 'citizen' in the second to the last line.
You mean, I. suppose, a British subject having domicile?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Any person who has acquired Canadian domicile by residing in Canada for three years would have the right to come back if he once went away.
What is a Canadian citizen as distinguished from a British subject?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We want a definition that will show' the distinction between a Canadian and a British subject who is not a Canadian, and we use the words 'Canadian citizen' for that purpose.
Then British subjects are not permitted to land in Canada as a matter of right?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, not because he is a British subject. He has to be either a Canadian citizen or he must have Canadian domicile before he can land in Can-, ada as a matter of _ right.
On section 23, jurisdiction of courts in cases of rejection and deportation re-I stricted.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is a new provision. It has been considered by the Justice Department so far as its form is concerned, but the policy of the section is a matter for the consideration of parliament. The Justice Department says that we have a legal right to pass such a section.
On section 25, passengers to be landed only at places designated by officer in charge-penalty for infraction,
Who imposes that fine?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is a provision in the latter part of the Bill.
Why is the very great latitude between the fine of $20 and $1,000 allowed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would depend on whether the Act was done with intent or with malice aforethought. There are possibilities in the case of steamers deliberately allowing prohibited passengers to get off at points where they would avoid detection and exclusion by our officers, and it is very necessary that there should be the power of a very drastic procedure in such cases. There are people who are prohibited from coming into Canada except on payment of a very high fee, and there is a great deal of money involved in the landing of such people free of charge. It is, therefore necessary that the punishment should be severe. If two Chinamen were landed outside the regular port of entry the saving would amount to this fine.

I am not objecting to the maximum, but I think the minimum is too low. It might be that it would be to the advantage of some transportation companies to be a little lax in their supervision of the landing of passengers because the passage money might exceed the amount of the possible penalty. My own observation in cases of this sort has been that as a rule the minimum and not the maximum penalty is applied. I do not know how the minister intends to have these new sections carried out. I suppose it will largely depend upon the instructions as to what the fines exacted shall be, but in my own experience I have found that the minimum fine is usually collected, and I think that $20 is too small.
This is intended to be the penalty with respect to each individual that shall be landed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
It should be applied to each individual who is landed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I would think it would be in each individual case, but this is not absolutely clear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
I would move that after the word 'dollars' in line 32 the words 'in respect of each such passenger or person' be inserted, and that the words 'in each case' in line 31 be struck out.
Section as amended agreed to.
